title: Gradual warming gave an early thermal-score lead that positive relaxation models cannot predict in a 2014 microalgae experiment
abstract: We tested a temperature-only lag explanation with data outside bird surveys and network summaries. A 2014 experiment supplied ten microalgae species to 144 flasks and compared equal-mean gradual and abrupt warming from 20 to 25 C. Separate growth assays gave species thermal scores. On day 28, gradually warmed communities had a higher biovolume-weighted score than abruptly warmed communities: +0.1393 assay C (95% joint bootstrap interval 0.0817 to 0.1987). By day 56 the contrast was -0.0787 (-0.1178 to -0.0459). Cell weights retained the reversal. Presence weights gave no clear late difference. Both signs remained after removal of each assayed species and in connected, isolated and homogeneous landscape subsets. We prove that every nonnegative mixture of linear exponential temperature responses with common initial states and nonnegative target gains predicts a nonpositive gradual-minus-abrupt contrast after these schedules end. The early positive contrast violates this order under those assumptions. This exploratory test shows that simple positive relaxation is insufficient here. It does not identify competition as the cause or estimate its share of the field climate-tracking gap. One laboratory system, two visits, assay transfer, nominal temperatures and unestablished chamber replication limit inference. Code, aggregate and unit-level derived evidence, source hashes and retrieval instructions are included.

display.caption: Independent growth assays define thermal scores. Gradual and abrupt warming from 20 to 25 C give opposite orders on days 28 and 56. Points are flasks; black bars are means. Flasks share paired landscapes and experimental chambers; points are not independent ecosystem replicates.

citations.reason: Weak spatial-to-temporal transfer motivates an independent experimental order test of a restricted lag model class. No network records or fitted summaries are reused.
Prior insecticide test did not explain the bird gap. Our experiment tests a different model restriction and does not partition the bird gap.

Source experiment. The original paper already found history effects on evenness and weak prediction of composition from monoculture assays. We add an independent-score reversal and a no-fit lag order test.
